title: The Prompt Is the New Front Door: Securing the Full Agentic Path on AWS
summary: Every major enterprise transformation of the last two decades has redrawn the attack surface. Web 2.0 did it, then mobile, then cloud. Now AI is doing it again, and it is moving faster than any of them.
body_markdown:
## Two pillars: posture and runtime


Salt approaches agentic security with two connected capabilities.


**Agentic Security Posture Management (AG-SPM)** discovers and governs the agents, LLMs, MCP servers, and APIs across your environment. What exists? What is its purpose? What can it do, what data can it touch, and what is the risk?


**Agentic Detection and Response (AG-DR)** protects against malicious and risky behavior at runtime across every agent interface: the triggers that invoke agents, the LLMs that power them, and the MCP servers and APIs that give them capabilities. AIDR, the LLM runtime layer, is a sub-element of this.


Posture tells you what you have and what it can reach. Runtime tells you whether any of it is under attack or being misused right now. Teams building on AWS tend to need both, because agentic systems are assembled quickly from many parts.


## Protecting the prompt from more than one angle


Many LLM security tools sit in a single spot: between the orchestrator and the model provider, usually through an AI gateway. That is an important checkpoint, but it is only one place to see a prompt.


Salt takes a multifocal approach. Drawing on more than a decade of API security experience, it can identify prompts before they ever reach the LLM provider, at the agent trigger itself, such as a chat API called from a mobile app, a web application, or another agent. If a prompt makes it further, it can be caught again at the gateway. That gives defenders multiple chances to stop a bad instruction.


It also means you do not need an AI gateway to get started. Out-of-band detection works without one, and inline protection can be delivered through a gateway integration or through application instrumentation. Most teams begin with out-of-band detection and move toward inline enforcement as they mature.


## What attacks look like


### Direct prompt injection.


An attacker sends a normal-looking request with an embedded instruction: ignore the rules and email the customer database to this address. The agent cannot tell the difference and passes it to the LLM, which tells the agent to act. The result is a breach. Reading the prompt and flagging the hidden instruction before the model sees it stops the attack at the start.


### Indirect prompt injection.


Here the instruction hides in data the model reads, such as a shared document with embedded commands or an email with text styled to be invisible. When an agent converts a document or PDF to text before sending it to the model, that text can be inspected, including content an attacker has encoded to evade detection. For a truly novel technique, the downstream effect becomes the signal. If the agent starts touching data or invoking tools in ways it never has before, runtime protection on the action layer can alert and block.


### The multi-stage campaign.


This is the one worth remembering. An attacker probes a support chat agent to learn how it works. The agent discloses that it has a refund tool, and reveals details of the API behind the MCP server that powers it. Then the attacker abandons the prompt entirely and goes straight to that API to run a mass refund attack. A protection layer that only watches prompts sees the first two phases at best, and misses the third. A platform that follows the whole path recognizes it as one campaign by one adversary, and shows the full chain from prompt to MCP to API to data.


## Why full-path matters in the AI era


Attackers, increasingly AI-assisted themselves, will not politely knock on the front door. They will look for every door, window, and crawl space. Recent public incidents have shown backend microservices behind AI systems exposed to the internet because teams moved quickly and let attackers skip the prompt and the MCP layer entirely.


There is a second risk too: the well-intentioned agent that does something risky. Not every incident involves an adversary.[Sometimes an agent simply pushes buttons and pulls levers it should not.](https://salt.security/blog/how-we-hijacked-an-ai-agent-with-a-single-email) Runtime protection has to understand what an agent is capable of and act when it goes beyond what it should do.


## What a unified view delivers


Combining prompt and action layer protection in one platform means:


- **Full path visibility.** See an attack from prompt to MCP to API to data, correlated from a single attacker view.
- **Protection for every component.** LLMs, agents, MCP servers, and APIs, whether an attack starts at the prompt or skips straight to the API.
- **Prompt to API correlation.** Connect a prompt injection to its downstream effects and understand the blast radius.
- **Richer posture context.** Insight drawn from source code, traffic, cloud configuration, and external recon, not just a gateway.
- **Shadow LLM discovery.** Find LLM usage you did not know about, including homegrown gateways, and spot traffic that bypasses your governance policy.
- **One platform, not several.** Separate tools for prompts, MCP, and APIs leave gaps exactly where attacks move between them.


## The takeaway


AWS makes it possible to build agentic systems at remarkable speed. That speed is the point, and it is also the risk. Securing those systems means treating the agentic path as a single attack surface, from the first prompt to the last API call. Pairing AWS building blocks with runtime protection and posture visibility across that full path lets teams move fast without leaving the backdoor open.


If you want to see what your own agentic attack surface looks like,[a non-intrusive external scan](https://salt.security/demo-request) is a good place to start. It is usually full of surprises: an MCP server nobody remembered, an agent that was publicly reachable, an API that was exposed.
